summary: Defines a DNS extension letting a name server include its identity in a response. This helps when anycast or load balancing makes it hard to know which server answered. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: When many servers share one address, this lets the one who answers sign their name.

questions: how to tell which dns server answered
how does nsid work with anycast
subtitle: A DNS option that lets a name server say which one of many identical-looking servers answered.

tldr.problem: When anycast or load balancing lets many name servers share one IP address, it is hard to tell which of them answered a query.
tldr.mechanism: A resolver sends an empty NSID option (EDNS option code 3) in its query, and a name server that honors it returns an identifier of its own choosing in the same option in the response.
tldr.outcome: The identifier is an opaque byte string whose contents the operator chooses. The option is hop-by-hop, so it is not passed along from one server to another.

today: RFC 5001 is a Proposed Standard from August 2007, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Which Server Answered?
sections.content:
With DNS anycast, load balancing and similar mechanisms, many name servers can share a single IP address. It then becomes hard to tell which one answered a particular query.

Existing ad-hoc mechanisms let an operator send follow-up queries, but those are not fully satisfactory: anycast routing may have changed, or the pool may sit behind extremely dynamic load-balancing hardware. Because a DNS query is idempotent and keeps no state, the RFC concludes that the only completely reliable way to learn the responder's identity is for the name server to include it in the response itself.
sections.plainLanguage: If you call a number and a different helper might pick up each time, calling back will not tell you who helped before. The helper has to tell you in the same call.

sections.title: How the Exchange Works
sections.content:
The mechanism is an EDNS option (see RFC 2671) carried in an OPT pseudo-RR. A resolver asks by sending an empty NSID option in its query, and it MUST NOT include any NSID payload data. A name server MUST ignore any payload it finds in a query.

A name server that understands the option and chooses to honor the request puts identifying information in an NSID option in the OPT pseudo-RR of its response. Including it is always optional. A name server MUST NOT send the option to a resolver that did not request it.

The mechanism is not limited to authoritative servers; it applies equally to recursive name servers.
sections.plainLanguage: You hold up an empty name tag. The server fills in its own and hands it back. A server never hands over a name tag to someone who did not hold one up.

sections.title: The NSID Option Format
sections.content:
The OPTION-CODE for NSID is 3. The OPTION-DATA is an opaque byte string, and its meaning is deliberately left outside the protocol.

User interfaces MUST read and write the payload as a sequence of hexadecimal digits, two digits per payload octet. The payload is binary data, so comparisons MUST compare the raw bytes, and copy operations MUST NOT assume the payload is null-terminated. Any resemblance to text is only a convenience.

The RFC explains the choice of hex: it must be possible to cut and paste an exact copy of the payload into email or web forms without distortion, and hexadecimal strings, while ugly, are robust. Text formats would drag in complex internationalization issues.
sections.plainLanguage: The name tag can hold any pile of bytes, so it is always shown as plain hex digits that cannot get scrambled when copied.

sections.title: Choosing the Payload
sections.content:
What goes in the payload is the server administrator's prerogative. The RFC lists possibilities, each with trade-offs:

  • The server's real name, which is simple, but a server may not have one.
  • The real IP address, which is simple, but the operator may not want to reveal its non-anycast address.
  • A hash or pseudo-random number, which is fixed length but is no help if its search space is small.
  • A probabilistically unique identifier kept across reboots, which avoids that search-space problem but cannot be mapped back to an instance by any algorithm.
  • An arbitrary string, which is one more setting to misconfigure; if every node says "My Name Server", it is not useful.
  • Signed or encrypted blobs, which need detailed security analysis the RFC leaves out of scope.

Since no single choice fits everyone, the payload is left opaque. The guidelines: operators who do not want to reveal a unicast address could use the raw binary form of a probabilistically unique random number, which should probably be the default behavior. Using a unicast address, or an arbitrary value, should only happen through an explicit configuration choice.
sections.plainLanguage: The server can use a name, an address or a secret code as its tag. Each has pluses and minuses, so the rules let the owner choose and suggest a random number as the safe default.

sections.title: Not Transitive, and Truncation
sections.content:
The NSID option is not transitive: it is strictly hop-by-hop. If a client asks a recursive name server for NSID, the recursive server identifies itself. If that server wants the identity of the servers it queries, it may add its own NSID requests, but that has no effect on what it returns to the original client. A transitive variant, letting a stub resolver learn which authoritative server supplied an answer, is left for future work.

Adding the option can trigger message truncation, though the specification does not change the DNS truncation rules and never requires a server to truncate. A resolver that requests NSID supports EDNS, so it can use the sender's UDP payload size field of the OPT pseudo-RR to advertise a buffer large enough to make truncation unlikely.
sections.plainLanguage: The tag only describes the helper you spoke to directly, not any helper that helper called. If the tag will not fit in the reply, the server can leave it out.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The RFC calls NSID a channel signaling mechanism intended primarily for debugging. Such mechanisms are outside the scope of DNSSEC, so applications needing integrity protection for the signaled data will need a channel security mechanism such as TSIG (RFC 2845).

Some payload contents are security sensitive in some environments, which is why content is left to the operator. For signed or encrypted payloads, implementors should seek competent advice first. IANA has allocated EDNS option code 3 for NSID.
sections.plainLanguage: The tag is meant for troubleshooting and is not locked against tampering. If you need it protected, use a separate lock. Some tags could give away secrets, so the owner chooses wisely.

messages.label: Query + empty NSID option
messages.note: Carried in the EDNS OPT pseudo-RR; no payload.

messages.label: Response + NSID option with identifier
messages.note: Optional; only sent because the resolver asked.
